lessons.title: Computing and virtual machines
lessons.outcome: Explain how a host, hypervisor, guest OS and application differ.
explanation: A physical server supplies processors, memory, network ports and storage access. A hypervisor divides these resources into virtual machines. Each VM has a guest operating system that runs applications.

A running VM is only one part of a working service. It may still need readable disks, a usable virtual network, identity, name resolution and a healthy application. Shared hosts create shared dependencies: several VMs can be affected by one host problem.

terms.meaning: The physical computer providing resources.
The layer that creates and runs virtual machines.
The operating system inside a VM.
Assigned processor capacity and memory; neither is storage space.

lessons.scenario: Three fictional application VMs stop together, but user laptops remain powered. Which shared dependency should you investigate?
options: The host and its resource/storage health
Only one user password
The color of a network cable
feedback: The shared host is a plausible common dependency. Check evidence before concluding it is the cause.
A single password does not explain three VMs stopping together.
Cable appearance is not evidence of host or application health.

lessons.title: Ethernet switching and VLANs
lessons.outcome: Distinguish local Layer 2 forwarding from routing.
explanation: A switch forwards Ethernet frames within a local network. A VLAN separates a switch network into logical broadcast domains. An access connection typically serves one VLAN; a trunk can carry multiple VLANs.

A matching cable connector does not prove the logical network is correct. Physical link state, VLAN membership, allowed VLANs and virtual-switch attachment are different questions. A VLAN alone is not a complete security policy.

terms.meaning: A Layer 2 unit of network communication.
An address used in Ethernet forwarding.
A logical Layer 2 broadcast domain.
A link carrying traffic for multiple VLANs under an agreed tagging design.

lessons.scenario: A fictional VM link is up, but the VM was attached to a different training VLAN. What is the useful next check?
options: Disable every security control
Compare intended VLAN membership and virtual-switch attachment
Replace the application database immediately
feedback: Removing safeguards does not establish the Layer 2 mismatch.
Compare intended and observed logical attachment before changing anything.
A database replacement is not justified by a VLAN mismatch.

lessons.title: IP routing and transport
lessons.outcome: Explain why a remote subnet needs a route and a return path.
explanation: Routers move packets between IP networks. Routing chooses a path toward a destination; switching provides local forwarding. One device may perform both roles, so identify the function rather than relying only on its label.

For a remote training service, investigate the local attachment, gateway, forward route, return route and policy. Reaching a router does not establish that the application, identity service or information exchange works.

terms.meaning: A Layer 3 unit carried across IP networks.
An IP network range used to identify local and remote destinations.
A next-hop router used to reach other networks.
A route for replies to reach the original sender.

lessons.scenario: A synthetic request reaches the remote training network, but replies cannot return. Which missing requirement best explains this?
options: More VM memory in every case
A different application logo
A usable return route
feedback: Memory pressure is a separate hypothesis requiring evidence.
Branding does not establish network reachability.
Request and reply paths both matter. Policy or service faults can also exist.

lessons.title: DNS, identity and shared services
lessons.outcome: Separate name lookup, sign-in and permission checks.
explanation: DNS translates service names and helps clients discover services. Active Directory Domain Services uses DNS to locate domain controllers. A network path can be working while discovery or sign-in is failing.

Authentication asks who the user is; authorization asks what that identity may do. Time synchronization and certificates can also matter to services. Investigate each dependency using approved synthetic evidence rather than treating every failed sign-in as a transport outage.

terms.meaning: Name resolution and service discovery.
Information about identities and resources.
Checking an asserted identity.
Deciding which actions an identity may perform.

lessons.scenario: A synthetic user reaches the application, signs in successfully, but is denied a restricted task. Which area best fits the evidence?
options: Authorization for that task
Assume all transport is down
Assume every server is powered off
feedback: Successful sign-in and a denied action point toward permission checks; inspect the actual denial.
An application response shows some connectivity, though not every path is proven.
A responding application is inconsistent with every server being off.

lessons.title: Storage: files, blocks and persistence
lessons.outcome: Explain NAS, SAN and the difference between capacity and performance.
explanation: File storage presents files and folders, commonly using SMB or NFS. Block storage presents addressable blocks to a host, commonly through iSCSI or Fibre Channel. These are access models and protocols, not proof of compatibility with a particular Army stack.

Capacity describes how much data can be held. Latency describes response delay, while IOPS describes operations per second. A VM can be powered on yet unable to use an unavailable disk. A storage virtual machine in ONTAP is a storage-management construct, not necessarily a guest compute VM.

terms.meaning: File access over a network.
Block-storage access through a storage network.
A logical block-storage device exposed to a host.
Response delay and operations per second.

lessons.scenario: A training VM is on and reachable, but its application cannot read the attached data volume. What should you investigate?
options: Whether the web page uses a dark theme
Storage availability, host access and the data path
Assume that reachability proves storage is healthy
feedback: Appearance does not explain inaccessible data.
Storage is a separate dependency; inspect evidence without destructive changes.
A reachable VM does not prove its attached storage is usable.

lessons.title: Firewalls and least-privilege policy
lessons.outcome: Explain why a route is different from permission to communicate.
explanation: A firewall evaluates traffic against security policy. PAN-OS policies can consider zones, addresses, applications, users and services. A routing decision and a security decision answer different questions.

For a fictional application flow, describe the source role, destination service, intended application and expected decision. Review synthetic policy and traffic evidence. Do not solve a denial by opening all traffic, and do not assume that a port number alone identifies every application.

terms.meaning: A logical grouping used in firewall policy.
A tracked communication exchange.
Conditions and actions governing allowed or denied traffic.
Allow only the access needed for the approved purpose.

lessons.scenario: A fictional route exists, but the simulated firewall records a denial for the needed application. What is the best next step?
options: Add a permanent allow-all rule
Disable logging and try again
Review the intended flow and the matching policy with its owner
feedback: An allow-all rule expands access beyond the approved need.
Removing evidence makes diagnosis harder.
Reconcile the required flow with approved policy; no live device is changed here.

lessons.title: Containers, orchestration and disconnected delivery
lessons.outcome: Distinguish an image, container, VM and orchestration platform.
explanation: A container packages an application and its dependencies while using the host operating-system kernel. A VM has its own guest OS. Containerization changes packaging and management; it does not remove network, storage or security requirements.

An orchestrator manages workloads across machines. Disconnected environments also need approved images, dependencies, registries and update processes available locally. An image starting successfully does not prove that data is durable or that the entire application works.

terms.meaning: A packaged template used to create a container.
A running isolated application process environment.
A platform coordinating workload deployment and lifecycle.
A service that stores and distributes container images.

lessons.scenario: A fictional disconnected lab cannot download a required image. Which planning gap should be addressed?
options: Approved local image and dependency availability
An automatic assumption that the software is incompatible
A request to expose the lab directly to the Internet
feedback: Stage approved artifacts and their dependencies using an authorized process.
A missing download does not establish compatibility or incompatibility.
Do not change a disconnected boundary to bypass an unmet dependency.

lessons.title: Recovery, backups and availability
lessons.outcome: Define restoration evidence rather than assuming redundancy is backup.
explanation: Availability keeps a service usable. Recovery restores service after a failure. Redundant paths, replicated data and saved recovery copies address different failure cases; identify which failure the design is intended to survive. This lesson is an editorial exercise; full standard-text review remains pending.

A recovery exercise should use synthetic data and record what was restored, which user task works again, and how long recovery took. A copy that has never been restored is not sufficient evidence that the mission outcome can be recovered.

terms.meaning: The target time to restore a service.
The target limit on recoverable data loss, expressed as time.
A demonstration that recovery data can be used.
Components that may be affected by one shared failure.

lessons.scenario: Two training VMs use the same physical host and data volume. What has not been established?
options: That the VMs have names
Independence from host/storage failure and tested recovery
That applications use computing resources
feedback: Names do not demonstrate resilience.
A shared dependency can affect both VMs; test the intended recovery outcome.
Resource use alone does not establish recovery.

lessons.title: Security across the whole stack
lessons.outcome: Identify separate controls for identities, systems, data and operations.
explanation: Protect the management plane as well as user traffic. Separate administrator privileges, keep approved software baselines, protect secrets, inspect relevant logs and test recovery. A firewall cannot compensate for every identity, host or application weakness.

Teach least privilege through an observable task: a test user completes an approved action and is denied an unapproved one. Vendor features and secure-looking diagrams do not establish authorization to operate, a current hardening baseline or technical interoperability.

terms.meaning: Interfaces used to administer systems.
An approved set of versions and settings.
Records that help establish what happened.
Several complementary protections across dependencies.

lessons.scenario: A fictional user can reach the training app. What is stronger evidence of appropriate access control?
options: Every user has administrator privileges
The network diagram uses a lock icon
Authorized actions succeed and unauthorized actions are denied
feedback: Universal administrator access violates least privilege.
An icon is not evidence of enforcement.
Test allowed and denied actions; document results and limitations.
